name: AI × Decentralized Trust: Kickoff of the LFDT AI Working Group
description:
AI is already in our pull requests — and agentic AI needs exactly what we build. Let's talk about both.

AI has already arrived in our repositories. It writes patches, reviews pull requests, and is often the first thing a newcomer asks about a codebase they don't understand yet. At the same time, agentic AI is arriving from the other direction — as a use case. Autonomous agents need identities they can prove, credentials others can verify, and a way to pay each other for the things they consume. That is our home turf.

LFDT has no shared position on either side of this yet. This meeting launches the LFDT AI Working Group and sets its scope together with the people who will do the work.

We will open three questions:

**How do we use AI when building LFDT projects? What** is allowed, what has to be disclosed, and what does it mean for provenance, licensing, DCO sign-off, and security review? The Linux Foundation's existing generative AI guidance is the floor — the question is what our projects need on top of it.

**Can AI help us grow our communities?** Review bots like CodeRabbit, automated triage of good first issues, and onboarding assistants promise a shorter path from first-time contributor to committer. Do they actually deliver that, or do they just add noise for maintainers to clean up? And if we want them, who runs them and who pays?

**Where does our work connect to the AI world?** Two neighbours at the Linux Foundation matter most: the Agentic AI Foundation (MCP, goose, AGENTS.md) and the x402 Foundation, which stewards payments over HTTP for agents. Agentic identity and agent-to-agent commerce are exactly where DLT belongs — and where LFDT projects should be visible.

This is a kickoff, not a keynote. Bring your opinions, your objections, and the problems you already have. We want to leave with an initial scope, a meeting cadence, and named volunteers for the first work streams.

Open to everyone: maintainers, contributors, TSC members, LFDT staff, and anyone from the wider Linux Foundation AI ecosystem. No prior involvement in LFDT required.

**Zoom Meeting Link**: [https://zoom.us/my/hyperledger.community.3?pwd=UE90WHhEaHRqOGEyMkV3cldKa2d2dz09](https://zoom.us/my/hyperledger.community.3?pwd=UE90WHhEaHRqOGEyMkV3cldKa2d2dz09)

name: Co-work + Network 002
(CS)²AI Online™ Seminar: Water Cybersecurity: Keeping It Pure
description:
In late July 2026, attackers reached into water and wastewater utilities in at least 12 US states. They exploited internet-exposed programmable logic controllers (PLCs), including Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100/1400, Schneider Modicon M340, and Siemens S7-1200 units. The attackers changed IP addresses and passwords to lock operators out of monitoring and control. In some cases they altered ladder logic in PLC project files. Utilities reported pressure loss and localized flooding, and operators had to fall back to manual operations. On July 30 the FBI and EPA issued a joint alert, and an Iran-linked group claimed responsibility.
The campaign follows a pattern that is years in the making. In 2023, CyberAv3ngers defaced Unitronics controllers at the Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa. In 2024, American Water, the largest regulated U.S. water utility, was hit by a cyberattack, and Arkansas City switched to manual operations after an incident. In 2025, Poland reported ICS intrusions at five water treatment plants. The attack surface hasn't changed much in that time. It is still exposed PLCs and HMIs, default or shared credentials, integrator-managed remote access, and small utilities with few security staff.
The attackers and vulnerabilities in the core OT control system and SCADA technologies are not the only pieces of the puzzle that has created this perfect storm. The way that Water Utility OT systems have been designed, constructed, built, commissioned, and managed without cybersecurity oversight or involvement over the last several decades presents another unique problem in this critical infrastructure sector. System Integrators and Engineering firms who have been at the core of these processes are not trained and are not generally aware of the cybersecurity requirements that should have been incorporated into these systems, and the recent advisory from CISA reinforce this part of the problem:
FBI, CISA Warn of Third-Party ICS Integrator Risks:
https://securitytoday.com/articles/2026/09/28/fbi-cisa-warn-of-third-party-ics-integrator-risks.aspx
Lastly, we will wrap the session with recent cybersecurity regulations in Water-adjacent sectors that hint that this may be brought into the Water Utility sector in the near future
This session looks at the following geo-political, technical, and sector-specific issues and ends with a case study for a practical 3-step process that has been proven to solve this issue with over a dozen successful implementations in the water/waste water industry:
1\. Geo\-political and Financial Gain motivations for why the US Water Utility Industry is being targeted
2\. Technical vulnerabilities that have allowed the attacks to work: How attackers find and take over exposed controllers and what the attacks do at the logic and network layers
3\. Unique challenges that have arisen over decades of not having cybersecurity\-in\-the\-loop as Water Utility OT Systems are designed\, constructed\, built\, commissioned\, and managed \(Systems Integrators and Engineering Firms lacking core cybersecurity knowledge and awareness
4\. What the sector needs moving forward \> How do we fix this?
⁃ Which defensive measures work: removing direct internet exposure, segmenting control networks behind secure gateways, strict access control lists, locking PLCs against unauthorized logic changes with key switches, verifying project file integrity, monitoring for configuration changes, and keeping manual operation ready
⁃ Review of a case study for how these challenges are being resolved with a practical and proven 3-step process >> Assess, Remediate, and Monitor/Manage
5\. How the federal response and the push for water\-sector security standards may shape utility obligations in the months ahead\.

name: How to build an enterprise-grade AI software factory
description:
Join Matar Peles, Field CTO at Port, for a hands-on session on turning AI coding agents into a fully automated, end-to-end delivery pipeline. Learn how to build a unified context layer, set up step-by-step factory agents, implement human-in-the-loop approvals for high-risk paths, and track pipeline efficiency, taking a ticket directly to pull request live.

We'll dig into:
- **Setting up the factory itself:** map the full process end to end, from the moment work arrives to the moment it ships, so the line has defined steps instead of disconnected automations.
- **A unified context layer:** pull signals from the tools your teams already run into the shared source of truth every agent reasons over: services, owners, dependencies and the standards that apply to each.
- **Factory agents for each step:** onboard an agent per step with a named owner and a scope of what it can touch, so you can connect the next one without rebuilding the line.
- **Human in the loop gates:** name which paths carry enough risk to stop for a person, route each one to whoever owns it, and write their decision back before the work moves on.
- **Insights and optimization:** track what the line ships, how much of it ran without a human, and which step is holding everything up.

Matar Peles is a field CTO at Port, where he shapes how the company connects product and market and guides its technical strategy in the field.
